A Donut to a Mushroom type Antenna - Why?
by R. James McCabe
ExtraOrdinary Technology
October, 2006
Page number(s):
42
Many researchers have noticed that Tesla's Patent No. 1,119,732 1 has a huge donut type antenna at the top of the tower. When Nikola built his Wardenclyffe wireless tower on Long
Island, New York, the donut was replaced by a dome or mushroom design.
There has been speculation as to why the change…
Is the dome just a better design?
Perhaps there is a benefit to having a large interior cavity at the top of the tower?
As usual the real reason isn't all that exciting. The original donut design was very expensive. The architects' presented Tesla with an estimate of $450,000 1 for the donut antenna. Tesla had to change the antenna to a more economical design.
—RJM

Perhaps the ever-broadening field of invention has never known a genius more successful in developing far-reaching and original inventions than Dr. Nikola Tesla, whose name is known in every corner of the globe for his scientific achievements.
Dr. Tesla was born in 1857 in Smiljan, Lika, border country of Austria-Hungary, His early education was obtained in the elementary school of his native place. He continued his studies in the public school in Gospic, Lika, and after spending a period of four years in the Lower Real School in Croatia, he graduated in 1873.
His parents originally desired him to study for the clergy, which can be readily understood when one considers that Dr. Tesla's father was himself a very noted clergyman and orator. Dr. Tesla said yesterday he hopes to have his apparatus completed within two weeks, and then will give a demonstration to the press.
For the last forty years Dr. Tesla has been the storm center of scientific controversy. Recognized in the early part of his career as the father of modern methods of generating and distributing electrical energy, and pre-dating even Marconi in his experiments with wireless, Dr. Tesla has been decorated by many governments for his accomplishments. In recent years, however, it has been his custom to announce at his annual parties the perfection of inventions which some scientists have challenged as fantastic.
The therapeutic device, Dr. Tesla said yesterday, is an improvement of an invention he perfected many years ago before his famous laboratory burned, about 1895. He said it will cure many internal disorders. He used it to advantage on his friend, Mark Twain, Dr. Tesla said.

New York, July 11 — (Associated Press) — The discovery of a force ray that would destroy an army 100 miles away, that would make A nation's defenses Impregnable, has been announced by the inventor, Dr. Nikola Tesla.
In the interests of peace, Dr. Tesla said he plans to place the ray at the disposal of the Geneva disarmament conference. He announced the invention yesterday, on the occasion of his 75th birthday.
The force ray, Dr. Tesla said, would consist of particles, driven electrically and projected in vast curtains, miles high and 100 miles long.
The speed of the particles — traveling at velocities of 50,000,000 volts — was described by him as giving the ray its destructive powers.
He said projecting plants, set up every 200 miles along a border, each shooting rays 100 miles on each side, would make the border impenetrable.
A fleet of 10,000 airplanes, flying into such a curtain, he said, would be destroyed.

Dr. Tesla Gives Home to an Errant Pigeon That Flew Into 40th-Story Room in Hotel
New York Times
February 6th, 1935
Early yesterday morning, not so long after it started snowing, an apologetic housekeeper on the fortieth floor of the Hotel New Yorker — one flight from the roof — telephoned down to the office that there was a bird in one of the unoccupied rooms. Apparently it had flown in a window which had been left partially open during the night, she explained.
When the management arrived on the scene the "bird" was perched on the top of a dresser, as unaccountable as Poe's raven, and twice as ambiguous. It was a homing pigeon with a leg band reading: "I. F. 34 N. U. 1286," and it seemed to have just got in after a long hard flight. It was caught and shut in a bathroom until its legband could be deciphered.
The news of it spread, however. At 7 o'clock, while the management was still trying to face the anomaly of the homing pigeons without a home, a chambermaid was repeating the story to Dr. Nikola Tesla, the 78-year-old scientist, in his thirty-third floor suite. Dr. Tesla, who is fond of pigeons, as the chambermaid knows from experience, promptly called the management and volunteered to take charge of the foundling.

Dr. Tesla Talks of Gas Turbines
by Nikola Tesla
Motor World
September 18th, 1911
Page number(s):
23, 37
So Confident, He Offers to Build Them for Motor Cars
Considers New Power His Greatest Invention.
Gas turbines of practical and efficient construction, light, flexible and in every way suitable for automobile propulsion, are not a dream of the future only but a probability of only a very few years hence. At least such is the conviction of Dr. Nikola Tesla, whose newly developed method of fluid propulsion, as he calls it, and which was illustrated and described in last week's Motor World, is attracting so much attention in scientific circles. Dr. Tesla himself considers it the greatest of all his inventions. By his own statement the scientist already has built, run and carefully tested internal combustion engines operating on the new turbine principle and so confident is he of the thorough practicability of the idea that on Friday of last week he informed a Motor World man that he would even be willing today to sign a contract to build and install turbines for automobiles. He readily admits, however, that he would like to have more time, considerable more time probably, in which to develop a method of combustion entirely suited to the turbine.

Dr. Tesla Visions the End of Aircraft in War
by Helen Welshimer
Every Week Magazine
October 21st, 1934
Page number(s):
3
The famous inventor's new beam of death could bring down a fleet of 10,000 planes at a distance of 250 miles, he claims, and it also would make obsolete the submarine.
"America Enters War!"
"United Stated Joins Allies!"
"Congress Declares War!"
The newsboys were screaming the headlines through the rainy April night. Men and women stood on corners, talking, talking, talking—
The drift of the days went on. Troop trains pulled out of the stations, from Centreville, Mississippi, up to Bangor, Maine. The drums throbbed and the trumpets blew. The ships sailed and the casualty lists came back. One by one, the gold stars replaced the white—
And 1917 drifted into 1918.
Dr. Nikola Tesla was in his laboratory trying hard to solve a problem of ages. Once in a while he raised his head to listen. Then he turned back to his experiments. He was going to end war!
The noted inventor, 78 years old now, already had 700 inventions to his credit. This was to be his greatest.
Years marched on. The fanfare and the drums were done. The dead were buried. The living came home.

Dr. Tesla's Honors
by Nikola Tesla
New York Herald Tribune
July 27th, 1937

147
To the New York Herald Tribune:
I have been a reader of your excellent paper for more than fifty years and feel much obliged to you for the pleasure and enlightenment derived from its perusal. Many of your admirable editorials are on my files. Under these circumstances it is unfortunate that your issue of Sunday, July 11, contained a report very injurious to me.
The particularly damaging statement is: "The decorations made very little impression on Dr. Tesla. 'They mean nothing - take them away,' said Dr. Tesla."
I should say that the expression on my face in the photograph accompanying the report, would be sufficient to disprove the above assertion. When it became necessary to clear the table I was very anxious that the precious objects be placed in safe hands and requested my old friend, George Scherff, auditor of the Union Sulphur Company, who was one of the honored guests, to take care of them. Moreover, as soon as I was free, I cabled His Royal Highness Prince Regent Paul of Yugoslavia and to His Excellency Dr. Eduard Benes, President of Czechoslovakia, expressing my profound gratitude for the rare distinctions conferred upon me and my great pride of possessing them. The Drama of Mr. Tesla
New York Herald Tribune
January 17th, 1943
Page number(s):
A8
Mr. Nikola Tesla, the "wizard," died the other day, and he left a lot of questions unanswered. His solid accomplishments were astonishing in their scope-more than nine hundred patents, including the transforming coil and the induction motor. But, important as were his accomplishments, he deserves attention as a dreamer. He had! always been absorbed by glimpses into the world of tomorrow, a world in which power would be transmitted by radio, in which science could make the desert blossom by what would amount to the touching of a button. There was no limit to the range of his imagination. He even envisioned airplanes, fighters and bombers and all, without engines. We cannot know, but it may be that a long time from now, when patterns. are changed, the critics will take a view of history that will bracket Tesla with Da Vinci. Or with our own Mr. Franklin. Or with Dr. Loeb, who came close to the secret of life. One thing is sure: This world, as we run il today, did not appreciate his peculiar greatness.
Mr. Tesla was eighty-five years old when he died. He died alone. He was an eccentric, whatever that means, A nonconformist, possibly. At any rate, he would leave his experiments and go for a time to feed the silly and inconsequential pigeons in Herald Square. He delighted in talking nonsense - or was it? It looked like a joke: a 2-foot-square bedspring with a skinny, 6-foot-long pivoted slat fastened on top. Finally, helicopter. like, it hovered motionless at a point 50 feet above the crowd.

by Nikola Tesla

October 8th, 1892

In the last issue of The Electrical World I find an article on my "Drehstrom" patent which appeared originally in Industries , and is, I believe, from the pen of the able editor of that journal. Some of the statements made are such as to cause an erroneous opinion to gain ground, which I deem it my duty to prevent — a disagreeable one I may say, as I do not like to express my opinion on a patent, especially if it is my own.
It may be, as the writer states, that the theory of the action of my motor advanced in my paper before the American Institute in May, 1888, is a clumsy one, but this theory was formed by me a number of years before the practical results were announced, the patents being applied for only after it was undoubtedly demonstrated that the motor could fairly compete in efficiency with the direct current motor, and that the invention was one of commercial value. Early Decision is Necessary for Preserving Adams Plant
Niagara Falls Gazette
December 29th, 1961
Time is growing short for a decision on the future — if there is to be any future — of the Edward Dean Adams power station on the upper Niagara River.
This ancient hydroelectric plant is the daddy of them all. It was the Adams plant which first transmitted alternating current 25 miles to Buffalo in 1896. This was accomplished because of the efforts of Nikola Tesla, who developed the polyphase alternating current motor, and George Westinghouse, who adapted the system for the Adams generators.
Some time next fall the Adams plant will be taken out of service for all time. It will no longer be needed.
It would be unfortunate if it were to be torn down or left idle and forgotten. It is a symbol of the electrical age. It deserves to be preserved and maintained as a museum or electrical hall of fame, call it what you will. The buildings could be adapted to provide space for a permanent industrial exhibit.
Niagara Falls would derive benefit from having such a showplace to add to attractions for visitors. Museums are doing very well in Cooperstown and other tourist centers.
Surely, there are people in the community and in the American electrical industry with the imagination and leadership to undertake such a project.

What, for example, is the significance of establishing a close connection between the terrestrial phenomenon known as the aurora borealis and the eruptions of the incandescent gases which constitute the photosphere of the sun? The theory is that the electrostatic charge of the earth responds by greatly quickened vibrations to the manifestation of energy on the surface of the sun. But this is simply telegraphy without wires across an interval of 92,000,000 of miles. It is practically instantaneous, too. This fact was recognized years before a ready explanation of it was found in the close correspondence between the velocity of the electric vibration and that of light. Edison and His Inventions
Yonkers Statesman
July 22nd, 1892
The story that Mr. Edison has invented something by which a city could be destroyed, for instance, by an enemy thirty miles away, is, of course, an absurdity. The only interesting thing about it is that it is generally believed in Europe that Edison has perfected some such wholesale agent of destruction. He has received in the past two or three months a number of letters, some of them from people in authority, asking what there is in the report, and one of the letters contained an intimation that an European government might be disposed to treat with him for the exclusive possession of the secret.
Mr. Edison has told his friends about this experience, and has added that he has but one secret, and that is the operation of his ore extractor, a secret which he expects will yield him several millions of dollars.
Whether the fairy-like suggestion of his that an enemy might be destroyed by an electrically-charged volume of water played from a hose, or whether the report was due to the the suggestion that the discovery of Nikola Tesla might be utilized in war, so as to cast a lightning bolt into an enemy’s town or upon an enemy’s ship, Mr. Edison does not know, but he is inclined to think that the report can be traced to one of these two sources.

Edison and Tesla
by Hugo Gernsback
Electrical Experimenter
December, 1915

If the recent cabled reports be correct, every American will note with great satisfaction the awarding of this year's Nobel prize in physics to Thomas A. Edison and to Nikola Tesla.
When Alfred Nobel, the multi-millionaire inventor of dynamite and nitroglycerine died in 1896, his will provided for a series of five annual prizes to the most deserving persons in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and for the best work done in the interest of universal peace.
These prizes have been regularly awarded since 1901, and the learned Academies of Sweden while admittedly well informed and fair as to the award of the prize, have in the past, we believe, overlooked several scientists who by all means were entitled to the prize long ere this.
We are quite convinced, for this reason, that this year's choice of Edison and Tesla will not only be acclaimed in the United States, but in the world over. For, if the world is indeb:ed to two physicists, Edison and Tesla are certainly the biggest single creditors.

Possibly, it might be done, but it is not likely that any contractor would take the job at present. Nevertheless there are great possibilities in concrete, as every one who has kept in touch with the march of events must know. In all probability the concrete house will be popular in the near future, not merely because of its cheapness but on account of its durability and for many desirable features. Edison Outdone
Boulder Daily Camera
March 4th, 1896
Page number(s):
2
Wizard Tesla Substitutes Dilute Air for Electric Light Filaments.
A more original genius than Edison, veritably a wizard, is his young disciple, Nikola Tesla, who was born in Servia, and found employment with Edison on landing in America. For small electric lights he dispenses with the filaments inside the bulbs, and makes dilute air do their work. He sends currents of high tension through space, without any conductor, at a voltage many times greater than that employed in electrocution. He receives in his person currents vibrating a million times a second, of two hundred times greater voltage than needed to produce death. He surrounds himself with a halo of electric light, and calls purple streams from the soil. His experiments are of the utmost promise to the industrial world. His aim is to hook man's machinery directly to nature's, pressing the ether waves directly into our service without the intervention or the generation of heat, in which such an enormous proportion of the energy goes to waste - 90 per cent in arc lighting, 94 in incandescent. - Pres. Andrews in Scribner's.

The diagram herewith shown gives the form of the new lamp. It will be seen that there is no carbon loop. BY EDWIN J. HOUSTON AND A. E. KENNELLY.
Mr. Thomas A. Edison, after numerous experiments on the Röntgen rays with about 150 different glass vacuum tubes, has communicated the following information to us for publication:
First. There is no apparent advantage in obtaining a very high vacuum in the Crookes tubes employed for obtaining shadowgraphs of metal gratings. The effect of a very high vacuum is to require a greater voltage to produce fluorescence. The best degree of vacuum seems to be that at which the internal luminescence or stria in the tube just disappear and fluorescence of the walls remains. The Röntgen rays are still produced even when internal striæ are observed, but are then much enfeebled.
Second. Thin walls are preferable to thick walls in the glass vacuum tubes. A thick wall will fluoresce more noticeably and become very hot. A thin wall will emit rays upon the photographic plate, but may scarcely fluoresce visibly and will remain very cool. This is proved by a number of experiments, of which the following is one: The tube of a shape roughly indicated in Fig. I has its walls blown thick in the zone of A C, but thin at B. Editorial Comments Regarding the Nikola Tesla Lecture in Chicago
Electrical World
September 2nd, 1893
Page number(s):
167
The lecture delivered by Mr. Tesla at Chicago on Friday evening of last week was a disappointment to those who expected to be entertained with brilliant experiments in luminous discharges, transmissions without wires, and other like subjects with which the name of Tesla is so intimately associated. In place of these experiments, his audience soon found out, what perhaps many of them did not know before, that the subject of the lecture was mechanical and electrical oscillators, a purely technical subject, involving but a few experiments, and these of little interest except to technical men; those of his audience who were not technical men were therefore disappointed; instead of being entertained they were being instructed with some matters not easily grasped by them. The apparatus forming the subject of his lecture was a true Tesla surprise, as will be seen from our brief report of the lecture. It consisted of a pneumatic oscillator, the underlying principle of which is analogous to that of the Leyden jar, the result accomplished being that it produced short, rapid, mechanical oscillations; but it differed in that these oscillations were of an absolutely constant frequency, as constant as that of a tuning fork, a feature which may make the apparatus quite a valuable one.

A bronze bust of Nikola Tesla, U.S. electrical engineer and pioneer in the field of electric motors and radio communications, now graces the entryway to Davies Auditorium in the Becton Engineering and Applied Science Center, 15 Prospect St.. This is the second time the Croatian-born inventor has been honored by Yale. In 1894, he received an honorary degree from Yale along with several other 19th-century leaders.
The Tesla sculpture was funded through a letter-writing campaign by a classroom of third-graders in Ann Arbor, Michigan, under the leadership of their teacher, John Wagner , who presented the sculpture to Yale on April 21. The students practiced their penmanship by writing letters to more than 100 American corporation leaders seeking donations.
D. Allan Bromley, dean of Yale engineering, noted that Tesla's discovery of the rotating magnetic field in 1888 enabled him to invent and patent the first practical system for generating and transmitting alternating current. Perfecting a generator that would give him currents of several thousand alternations per second, and inventing his disruptive discharge coil, he has created electrostatic conditions that have already modified not a few of the accepted notions about electricity.

America is by far the largest user of electric light, but the methods of production and utilization in use here do not appear to be quite so economical as those practised abroad. The plants throughout Europe are generally on a much more modest scale than here, except in a few such cities as Berlin, Hamburg, and Vienna, yet recent statistics show that some of the smallest are competing successfully, not only with long established gas-works, but with petroleum. Very little of the current, however, is used for power purposes, and conveniences like the fan motors now running daily by the hundred thousand in the United States are well-nigh unknown; so much so that when needed they are shipped from New York. In Berlin 19.9 per cent. of the current is employed in lighting dwellings and hotels, but in Hamburg the same item runs up to 38.7 per cent. Store lighting in the larger German and Austrian cities averages 80 per cent. of the current. Berlin and Vienna use much less than 10 per cent. of the current for driving motors in factories, stores, etc. Exceedingly little use is yet made of the current for heating. A large proportion of the stations have storage-battery equipments; in America this auxiliary is almost unheard of in central-station operation, though nobody appears to know why.

Dr. H. R. Humphries, neurologist at the Post Graduate Hospital, does not think very highly of Nikola Tesla's scheme to improve the mental condition of defective children by electric stimulation. As a neurologis for ten years at the Vanderbilt Clinic and for five years at the State Hospital for the Insane, Dr. Humphries has had experience with mental diseases and he feels very strongly on this particular subject.
"As I understand the proposed scheme," he said, "the plan is to charge the walls of the schoolroom where the defective children are with electricity and so to set up in the air a high grade frequency current. It is believed that this current will stimulate the cerebral cells of the defective child and so improve mentality. The proposition is silly.

ALBANY, April 9. — Frank W. Hawley was here to-day and extended to Gov. Morton an invitation to be present and officiate at the opening of the National Exposition of Electrical Appliances, to be held at the Grand Central Palace, in the city of New York on May 5th.
The Governor’s part in the great event will be the turning on of a current of electricity generated at the Falls of Niagara and transmitted a distance of 472 miles over one of the commercial wires of the Western Union telegraph, the new “Tesla” system of long distance transmission being employed.
The current will operate a large model of the Niagara power plant and a model of the cable-way system of canal boat propulsion. This is the longest transmission of power ever accomplished. The nearest approach to it was a transmission over a line in Europe 110 miles long.
Another feature of the exposition as explained to the Governor will be the placing of a large receiver at the brink of the Falls and a transmitter in the exposition building, enabling those witnessing the application of this mysterious energy to the movement of machinery to hear the roar of the great cataract that produces it.

An Electrical Convention
New York Times
August 21st, 1889
Page number(s):
2
At the last meeting of the Connell of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers the action of the preceding meeting was reviewed, and instead of a committee of five, the President was directed to appoint a committee of fifteen to form a plan of organization for an international electrical convention to be held in this city coincident with the World's Fair of 1892. Secretary R. W. Pope was instructed to inform President Mascart of the electrical conference at Paris of this action, and to suggest that the unfinished work of the present conference be taken up at the proposed conference of 1892.
The following were elected delegates to represent the institute at the Paris conference now in session: Thomas A. Edison, E. Wilbur Rice, Jr., Carl Hering, Joseph Wetzler, and Nikola Tesla. All of them are now in France or on the way there. President Elihu Thompson will in a few days announce his appointments on the committee of fifteen and the work of organization will then be taken up. An invitation will be extended to all the electrical organizations of the country to participate in the proposed international conference.

NEW YORK, Aug. 17. — A patent has been granted to Nikola Tesla for an invention which, if his claims are borne out, will prevent the escape of electricity from a wire. Cortland Standard
May 15th, 1896

The present electrical exhibition in New York is the most important and interesting of the kind ever held. Among its main features will be exhibited for the first time on a large scale Tesla's invention for telegraphing around the world without a wire or metallic circuit. If it is successful, the world will need no more telegraph poles or ocean cables. Tesla has also succeeded in producing an electrical current of 10,000,000 volts, which he declares is perfectly harmless. The sight of machinery whirling and spinning by means of power brought from Niagara falls, 450 miles away, is enough to make anybody be thankful he lives in this age and generation. Edison's fluoroscope, in which the visitor may see the skeleton frame of his hands and arms, is calculated tο make one feel creepy.

They Expect Edison, Tesla and Pupin at Their Convention
Great Barrington, Mass, June 18. — The first detachment of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, who are to hold their annual convention here the present week, arrived by special train from New York. There were 100 engineers in the party. An additional hundred will arrive when the convention will be called to order in the town hall.
The entire early summer colony turned out to meet the engineers at the railway station. There was an interminable procession of carriages and the local committer, comprising the principal citizens of the town, was kept busy assorting the engineers and sending them away to their respective hotels.
The convention will hold morning sessions daily until Saturday, when the engineers will return to New York, on a special train. It is expected that Thomas A. Edison, Nicola Tesla and Professor Pupin will be present. The Town Hall is beautifully decorated with evergreens and electric bulbs in honor of the occasion.

New York Press
April 3rd, 1892

Nikola Tesla was born at Smiljan, a small place on the Austrian border, and is now 35 years of age. His education was received at Carlstadt in Croatia; he showed the experimental beat, and eventually entered the polytechnic school in Gratz, Austria. Here he studied engineering and devoted his spare time to studying electricity. On graduation he entered the engineering department of the telegraph at Budapest. His recent lectures before European authorities and his ingenious electrical inventions have made him famous. His New York laboratory is one of the best equipped in the country.

Ray! Ray! Ray!
C-O-L-U-M-B-I-A.
Edison.
With such hearty welcome was "the Wizard of Menlo Park" received when he entered the lecture room of Havemeyer Hall, at Columbia University last night.
Nikola Tesla was giving experimental demonstrations with an electric oscillator when he saw Mr. Edison entering. His own greeting had been generous and hearty. When he saw the greatest of all American Inventors Mr. Tesla stopped his work and grasped Mr. Edison's hand, which he shook as he led him to a seat. The great audience appreciated the courtesy of the younger man and responded with cheers for both.
The American Institute of Electrical Engineers held what it was pleased to call a "conversazione" at Columbia University last night. In reality it was an electrical exposition, and the most complete ever known in America. Fully two thousand guests had been invited, and few of those that received invitations failed to attend. Half-tone Picture Transmitted by Wire from Chicago to New York.
NEW YORK, April 13. — Two bodies of scientific men gathered last night — one in Columbia College, this city, and the other in the rooms of the Quadrangle in Chicago, to witness the test of an electrical Instrument which was to transmit the half-tone picture by wire of President Seth Low to the Chicagoans and that of President Harris to the New Yorkers. The experiment was a success at the New York end, and 8,000 people gathered in the hall and watched the features of the President of the Chicago University evolve out of a maze of pin points in tin foil till it became a facsimile of the one on the transmitter, 1,000 miles away.
Chicagoans Disappointed
The Chicago audience however, according to word received by telegraph, was disappointed. The instrument at that end did not work because of heavy Induction in the wires.
R. H. Palmer operated the electrical machine transmitting the picture. The instrument contains tin foil perforated with countless pin holes each containing a separate wire. The paper upon which the picture is produced is wrapped around a cylinder upon which the sensitive tin foil stylus makes the ink dots corresponding in light and shade to the half-tone picture being transmitted.

The wonders of electricity have often been discussed with lively interest. This has been called the electrical age, because of the extraordinary developments in applying the subtle current to practical and beneficent purposes. But evidently we are only in the initial stages of electrical progress. That at least is the opinion expressed by those who have devoted their lives to studying and experimenting in the electrical world. No one has attained greater prominence in this line of activity than Nikola Tesla. Hence what he says, even if clothed in what seems to the average reader the language of extravagance, is certain to command attention.

Electrical Phenomena
Progressive Batavian
1893
In one of his remarkable lectures, Tesla states that most scientific men now look upon the various forms of manifestations of energy, which are generally designated "electric," as energy manifestations of the same nature as those of radiant heat and light. The phenomena of light and heat, and others besides, may therefore be called electrical phenomena, and thus it is that electrical science has become the mother science of all, and its study all-important. The day when we shall know exactly what electricity is will chronicle an event probably greater and of more moment than any other recorded in the history of the human race.

May 14th, 1894
Electrical Possibilities. It is not an extravagant statement to say that never before in the history of the world has there been a scientific discovery about which centered such magnificent dreams as are being built up on certain recently discovered electrical principles. "Among these the foremost place," says the Springfield Republican , must be given to the astounding discoveries of the young Serbian genius, Nikola Tesla, which are so novel and so extraordinary that the most imaginative of inventors are unable to foresee what form their development will take. Just as experimenters were beginning to think that they knew all that could be learned about electricity, and that further improvement must be in the line of more perfect mechanical application, Mr. Tesla shows us the electric fluid under conditions in which it differs from ordinary electricity as much as light differs from heat. A current of 2,000 volts will kill a man in the twinkling of an eye, but this modern wizard lets currents pour through his hands with a potential of 200,000 volts, vibrating 1,000,000 times a second and showering from him in dazzling streams of light. For some time after the experiment ceases his body and clothing emit streams and halos of splintered light.

Nikola Tesla Allows a Charge of 200,000 Volts to Pass Through His Body.
"I am convinced that I can today send a message to a ship at sea, and that those on board can understand it. If I cannot, I am willing to lay my head on the guillotine."
Nikola Tesla.
It was Nikola Tesla who made the above strange remark, and his wonderful achievements in the development of electrical science make his words worthy of respectful consideration. He has already established the fact that but one wire is necessary to create an electrical current and is now engaged on the problem of transmitting a current without the use of a wire at all. That he has grasped the secret of how this may ultimately be accomplished some of the experiments exhibited at his public lectures would seem to demonstrate.
Tesla produces a distinct and powerful glow without the aid of wires or globes and with apparatus remarkable chiefly for its simplicity. This consists of two highly charged disks; between which the light appears without a connecting fila ment of any kind. Electrical World
February 15th, 1890
Page number(s):
106
While a large portion of the European family has been surging westward during the last three or four hundred years, settling the vast continents of America, another, but smaller, portion has been doing frontier work in the Old World, protecting the rear by beating back the "unspeakable Turk" and reclaiming gradually the fair lands that endure the curse of Mohammedan rule. For a long-time the Slav people - who, after the battle of Kosovopolje, in which the Turks defeated the Servians, retired to the confines of the present Montenegro, Dalmatia, Herzegovina and Bosnia and "Borderland" of Austria - knew what it was to deal, as our Western pioneers did, with foes ceaselessly fretting against their frontier; and the races of these countries through their strenuous struggle against the armies of the Crescent, have developed notable qualities of bravery and sagacity, while maintaining a patriotism and independence unsurpassed in any other nation.
It was in this interesting border region and from among these valiant Eastern folk that Nikola Tesla was born; and the fact that he, to-day, finds himself in America and is one of our foremost electricians is striking evidence of the extraordinary attractiveness alike of electrical pursuits and of the country where electricity enjoys its widest application.

In the Electrical World - Tesla's Remarkable Lecture
Progressive Batavian
1893
In one of his remarkable lectures, Tesla states that most scientific men now look upon the various forms of manifestations of energy, which are generally designated “electric,” as energy manifestations of the same nature as those of radiant heat and light. The phenomena of light and heat, and others besides, may therefore be called electrical phenomena, and then it is that electrical science has become the mother science of all, and its study all-important. The day when we shall know exactly what electricity is will chronicle an event probably greater and of more moment than any other recorded in the history of the human race.

Electricians in This City Regard the Hunter Patents as Amusing
New York Herald
December 22nd, 1897
Page number(s):
3
Electricians in this city do not take Rudolph M. Hunter seriously. They say he will patent anything regardless of its practicability, and probably ranks seventh among men and corporations in the number of his patented electrical devices. He is credited with having taken out more than four hundred patents.
I explained to Nikola Tesla, in his laboratory at No. 46 East Houston street, yesterday. Mr. Hunter's latest patents. He was greatly amused.
"I could tell a whole lot about Mr. Hunter and his numerous patents," he said, "but it might appear that I am antagonistic to him, which is not so.
"His contention that his patents cover the alternating principle of transmitting electrical energy is silly. This method dates too far back to be patented as a system. I do not think his claims will prove an important factor in the electrical world or a disturbing element in the methods now in use."
At the offices of the Westinghouse Company, No. 120 Broadway. Mr. Hunter's patents were treated as amusing.
"We know Mr. Hunter very well," said Mr. Terry, the patent attorney of the company. "These transformer patents amount to little. We own six thousand of the ten thousand patents covering electrical devices. We are working under them and shall continue to work under them."

Electricians Show Interesting Exhibits
New York Press
April 13th, 1901
Page number(s):
3C
Tesla Gives Demonstrations of His Latest Invention.
TRANSMITTING PICTURES BY WIRE
Test Fails Because of Induction, but Success Hoped for Today — Edison and John D. Rockefeller Present.
Of more than usual interest to the general public is the conversazione held yesterday in Columbia University by the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. Many new and important inventions were shown and original and interesting experiments were made. The exhibits fill twelve rooms and represent the work of fifty eminent scientists. Among them is Nikola Tesla.

A patent has been granted to Nikola Tesla for an invention which, if his claims are borne out, will prevent the escape of electricity from a wire. Tesla's invention, it is claimed, solves the insulation problem in a simple manner. He insulates the wire by passing through it, or near it, air kept at a low temperature, producing a coat of ice on the wire, which, the inventor finds, cannot be broken through by the strongest current, and at the same time gives an insulation that costs practically nothing. By means of this latest discovery the loss of electricity or electrical energy in transmission, it is claimed, can be rendered so small as to be insignificant, and power can be transmitted to great distances by means of underground wires.

The test of electricity as a motor power on the canals of the State will probably be made at Pittsford on the Erie Canal near Rochester, Saturday, November 11th. The revolutionary character and vast financial possibilities of a practical commercial battery producing electricity directly from coal, without the intervention of boiler and steam engine, is obvious enough to the merest tyro in mechanics. Theoretically, such a coal battery might have an efficiency of something like 70 per cent., whereas existing methods of producing electrical energy, according to W. R. Cooper, only render available 6 per cent. of the energy of the coal. This fact, combined with the possibility of greatly reducing the cost of an electric plant, through the elimination of engines, boilers, and a number of the skilled workmen necessary to keep them in running order, makes the coal battery an intensely fascinating problem for the inventor.

The following will be the weekly schedule of lectures upon the Electricity Department of the World’s Fair. They will be delivered at 10 o’clock each day in the Agricultural Assembly Hall by Prof. Gooch.
On Mondays there will be discussed the principles of primary batteries, storage batteries, electric furnace, electro-plating, electric engraving, and Edison’s last invention, the Kinetograph.
Tuesdays — The telegraph, telephone, phonograph, telautograph, Atlantic cable system, and cooking and heating.
Wednesdays — Edison system of lighting.
Thursdays — The alternating system and Nikola Tesla’s theory of utilizing the power of Niagara Falls.
Fridays — Arc lighting, welding and drilling.
Saturdays — Electric street car system.
The purpose of the lectures is to give an intelligent understanding of the principles of the various apparatus on exhibition, the manner of their construction and practical operation. The class is open to all persons who desire an explanation of the wonderful developments of electricity and the various applications to which it may be adapted.

August, 1892

An interesting example of electric-power transmission is that of the Gold King stamp-mill near Telluride, Col. A Pelton wheel, receiving water through a two-foot steel pipe under 320 feet head, drives the generator at a speed of 833 revolutions, giving 10,000 alternations per minute. The generator, by an automatic compensation, is made to maintain a constant pressure of 3000 volts at the motor, three miles distant. The line runs 2500 feet directly up the mountain from the power station, and thence passes over a rough, and in winter almost inaccessible, country, to the mill. The working motor, being of the synchronous type, requires a special device for starting it, and this is furnished by a small auxiliary motor of the Tesla type. The operation of starting is accomplished by one man in about two minutes. The economical efficiency of the synchronous motor system, exclusive of loss in conductors, is found to be 83.5 per cent. at full load and 74 per cent. at half load. The capacity of the motor is 50 horse-power. It seems to me that there are interesting possibilities in the training of animals by electricity. Of course, it's rather out of my province, but the idea of the electrical subjugator appears feasible when one knows the power of electricity and the instinctive fear that brutes have of the unknown. Willard E. Case's announcement before the New York Electrical Society at Columbia College that he can produce electricity from carbon without heat has caused some stir among the men who are devoting their time to the development of electricity.
He cited the fact that the generation of energy through heat involves a waste of more than 75 per cent, and that all electricity except that produced by water power or galvanic battery is obtained ultimately from carbon.
Nikola Tesla was seen to-day and asked what his views were concerning Mr. Case's new road to electricity.
"The process of converting the energy of combining carbon and oxygen with electricity without any loss in the battery is not new," he said, "It has been observed that In the process there is no weakening of temperature shown, consequently there seems to be no loss in heat.

On the contrary, I am convinced that the second law of thermo-dynamics is far more general than it is believed to be. As long, however, as we contine ourselves to developing energy by consuming material we are adhering to barbarous processes which imply destruction and waste.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD: —
In reply to your question as to what discovery would do most to better our condition, in my opinion the demonstration that the earth's electrical charge can be distributed, and thereby electrical waves efficiently transmitted to any distance without the use of cables or wires, would be the most beneficial.
The conveying of motive power from sources such as Niagara in this manner to any place, however remote, would increase many times the productive capacity of mankind. It would bring millions of miserable creatures from the darkness of the coal pits to the light of day. It would cause a kinder feeling to spring up between the weak and the strong, which would lead to a generous adjustment of the evermore difficult questions of labor and capital.
Even if power could not be distributed, the mere transmission of intelligible signals would be of incalculable benefit. An atom of hydrogen consists of a thousand "electrons" — mere charges of electricity. An atom of lead consists of some hundreds of thousands of such "electrons'. That is why hydrogen is so light and lead so heavy. Each is drawn to that great mass of matter, the earth, in proportion to the number of electric charges which make up the earth. Electro-Motors
by Nikola Tesla
Electrical Review
April 3rd, 1891
Page number(s):
446
Fifteen or sixteen years ago, when I was pursuing my course at the college, I was told by an eminent physicist that a motor could not be operated without the use of brushes and commutators, or mechanical means of some kind for commutating the current. It was then I determined to solve the problem.
After years of persistent thought I finally arrived at a solution. I worked out the theory to the last detail, and confirmed all of my theoretical conclusions by experiments. Recognizing the value of the invention, I applied myself to the work of perfecting it, and after long continued labor I produced several types of practical motors.
Now all this I did long before anything whatever transpired in the whole scientific literature — as far as it could be ascertained — which would have even pointed at the possibility of obtaining such a result, but quite contrary at a time when scientific and practical men alike considered this result unattainable. In all civilized countries patents have been obtained almost without a single reference to anything which would have in the least degree rendered questionable the novelty of the invention. The first published essay — an account of some laboratory experiments by Prof. Ferraris — was published in Italy six or seven months after the date of filing of my applications for the foundation patents. An Electrolytic Clock
by Nikola Tesla
Electrical Engineer
May 6th, 1891
Page number(s):
517
If a delicately and pivoted and well-balanced metal disc or cylinder be placed in a proper plating solution midway between the anode and cathode, one half of the disc becomes electro positive and the other half electro negative. Owing to this fact metal is deposited on one, and taken off from the other half, and the disc is caused to rotate under the action of gravity. As the amount of metal deposited and taken off is proportionate to the current strength, the speed of rotation, if it be small, is proportionate to the current.
Tesla's Electrolytic Clock
The first device of this kind was operated by me early in 1888, in the endeavor to construct an electric meter. Elsa Maxwell's Party Line - An Electron Never Lies
by Elsa Maxwell
New York Post
December 30th, 1942
Page number(s):
10
One of the great new developments of modern years is electronics—the science of the movement of the electron through gaseous tubes.
I know this sounds like a mouthful. It also sounds unimportant. But in this strange and relativistic world, it is really the fantastic, the microscopic and the unbelievable which is important. I happen to be very much interested in the electron; and I’m interested for the same reason that I’m interested in Bach, Cézanne, steak Chateaubriand and pandas. The electron is part of the slipstream of living.
Look at what we , with our uniquely American mechanical genius, are doing: We are taking the almost-imperceptible electron, slipping it into harness, sending it up to detect airplanes, sending it down from airplanes to detect submarines, shooting it through smokestacks to detect and measure tell-tale smoke.
But recently , in the Westinghouse Lamp Laboratories at Bloomfield, N. J., I saw what to me is one of the strangest and most awesome demonstrations of electronics yet to be made: something that puts even the marvels of television into the shade. I saw a Klystron in action.
